::: {.why}
Ranking, z-scoring and winsorizing look like preprocessing and each one changes which positions dominate the portfolio, which means each is a modelling choice you should be able to defend.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Say what a rank transform assumes about the relationship between signal magnitude and expected return, and when that assumption costs you.
- Report the effect of three transforms on the same signal's Sharpe, turnover and concentration.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>60 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Implement the transforms in qlib/signals/transforms.py: cross-sectional z-score, cross-sectional rank mapped to a normal, and winsorised z-score at a stated quantile. Each declares what it does to units, since the interface from day 162 requires it.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Run the comparison: one signal, three transforms, reporting Sharpe, turnover, the weight of the largest position, and the fraction of profit coming from the top 5 percent of names. Ranking throws away magnitude, which helps when the tail is noise and hurts when the tail is where the information is, and this table tells you which case you are in.
:::
:::
